questions.q: Why does the lab use np.allclose(result, plus) instead of result == plus to check the X @ plus calculation?
options: np.allclose is required because == does not exist for NumPy arrays at all
Floating-point results can differ by tiny rounding amounts between computation paths, so np.allclose checks 'close enough within tolerance' instead of requiring exact bitwise equality
np.allclose always returns True regardless of the actual values, so it is used purely for convenience
result == plus would raise an error if the arrays contain floats
questions.explain: Floating-point arithmetic can produce values like 0.7071067811865475 that differ in the last bit depending on how they were computed. np.allclose compares within a tolerance, which is the correct way to check float array equality; exact == is unreliable for this.

questions.q: What condition defines a unitary matrix U, and why does it matter physically for a quantum gate?
options: U @ U.conj().T must equal the identity matrix; physically this guarantees the gate preserves total probability rather than creating or destroying it
U must have all real entries, with no exceptions
U's determinant must always equal 0
U @ U must equal the zero matrix
questions.explain: Unitarity (U @ U.conj().T = I) is the mathematical condition that guarantees a gate only redistributes probability among outcomes rather than changing the total -- the defining requirement for any valid quantum gate matrix.

questions.q: For the Hadamard matrix H, the lab notes that H.conj().T equals H.T. Why is that specifically true for H but not necessarily for every matrix?
options: H.conj().T equals H.T for every possible matrix, with no exceptions
This is a coincidence specific to the Hadamard matrix and would not hold for any other real matrix
H has entirely real entries, so complex conjugation (which only affects imaginary parts) has no effect on it, leaving just the transpose
H is a 2x2 matrix, and conjugation only applies to matrices larger than 2x2
questions.explain: Conjugation flips the sign of imaginary parts. Since every entry of H is real (no imaginary component to flip), .conj() does nothing, so .conj().T reduces to just .T. This would be true of any real-valued matrix, not just H specifically.

questions.q: For Pauli-Y = [[0,-1j],[1j,0]], the lab computes Y @ Y.conj().T and verifies it equals the identity matrix using full complex arithmetic. Why was skipping the .conj() step (using only Y @ Y.T) not a safe shortcut here, unlike for Hadamard?
options: Y.T and Y.conj().T are always identical for any matrix, so it would have made no difference
Pauli-Y cannot be transposed because it is a complex matrix
The .conj() step is purely cosmetic and never affects any numeric computation
Y has genuinely imaginary entries, so omitting .conj() would fail to flip the sign of the imaginary parts, producing a different (and incorrect) result than the true conjugate transpose requires
questions.explain: Unlike Hadamard, Y's entries include ±1j. .conj() is required to actually flip those imaginary signs; using only .T on Y would skip that step and not correctly reconstruct Y's true conjugate transpose, so the unitarity check would not come out right.

questions.q: In Task 3, np.kron(ket1, ket0) produces [0, 0, 1, 0], a 4-element vector. What does this confirm, consistent with the Kronecker product lesson?
options: This result indicates an error, since kron of two length-2 vectors should produce a length-2 result
The two qubits remain in two separate 2-dimensional spaces, only visually concatenated
Combining two 2-dimensional single-qubit states via np.kron produces one 4-dimensional two-qubit state vector representing |10>
np.kron always returns a 2x2 matrix regardless of its inputs
questions.explain: np.kron(ket1, ket0) = [0,0,1,0] is a single 4-dimensional vector (shape (4,)), with the 1 in position 2 -- the binary number '10' -- confirming that two 2-dim single-qubit vectors combine multiplicatively into one 4-dim joint state, as established in the Kronecker product lesson.
